What helps everyone feel comfortable:
- Clear, posted norms: quiet hours, clean-up after yourself, keep paths clear, close the gate so kids don’t run out, no slurs or harassment—ever. Same rules for everybody, no exceptions for “regulars” or for folks with money.
- Multilingual and visual: signs in Spanish/English (and others if we can), pictures for key rules, and a buddy system so new neighbors aren’t lost.
- Small, steady gestures: learn names, pronouns if people share them, share food without making it a test, and keep invitations open—“bring your partner/family/friend,” no assumptions.
- Privacy as a baseline: we don’t gossip about health, papers, or people’s pasts. If someone shares, we treat it with care.

On specific situations:

Alcohol or substance struggles:
- We judge behavior, not people. If someone is intoxicated in the garden, we check they’re safe, offer water and a seat, and make sure tools are put away so no one gets hurt.
- We set boundaries: no using in shared family spaces, no open containers around kids, and keep glass out.
- We keep resource cards handy for support services. Some neighbors choose to get trained on overdose response and keep naloxone; that’s about saving lives, not shaming. If there’s immediate danger, we call for help.

Infectious diseases:
- We don’t ask folks about diagnoses. We use universal care: wash hands, don’t share cups or cigarettes, wipe down shared tools, cover cuts, stay home if you’re actively sick.
- Masks are always okay—no comments. We follow public health guidance if there’s an outbreak.
- We make it easy to be safe: hand gel by the hose, paper towels, labeled bins.

Different racial, religious, linguistic backgrounds:
- We meet people where they are—slow down our speech, use translation apps, build a volunteer list of bilingual neighbors so the same person isn’t translating every time.
- We celebrate without putting anyone on display. If someone offers to share a tradition, we make space; we don’t demand it.
- If there’s a careless comment, we correct gently but firmly: “We don’t talk about people like that here.”

LGBTQ+ neighbors, unmarried couples, different family shapes:
- Treat every family the same. No intrusive questions about relationships or bodies. If someone shares their pronouns, we use them; if they don’t, we don’t force it.
- Our code of conduct covers slurs and harassment. First a private reminder, then mediation if needed.

Where we need extra communication and tolerance:
- Noise and celebrations: people mark holidays differently. We set quiet hours with room for occasional events if neighbors are notified. Put big gatherings on a shared calendar.
- Smells—food, incense, smoke: we can designate smoke-free zones and times, and talk about ventilation instead of shaming traditions.
- Kids and safety: agree on basic supervision, tool storage, and locked gates. Many hands prevent accidents.
- Pets: leashes, cleanup, and a plan for dogs who are nervous around kids.

Why this matters:
- People carry shame around addiction, fear around illness, trauma from past discrimination, or worry about police and immigration. Clear, fair rules and a culture of “ask first, assume good intent” lower the temperature so folks aren’t defensive.
- Consistency builds trust. If the rules are the same for the pastor’s wife, the young guys who just moved in, and the old timer on the corner, people relax.

How we handle problems:
- Step 1: friendly check-in—“Hey neighbor, can we talk about the music after nine?”
- Step 2: bring a neutral buddy if it’s awkward.
- Step 3: short group check-in at the garden once a month to adjust what’s not working.
- Step 4: if someone’s safety is at risk, we act fast and call the right help.

My bottom line: we don’t need everyone to be the same; we need the space to be safe enough for differences. Nos cuidamos—we take care of each other—with warm hearts and firm boundaries. That’s how people breathe easier and keep coming back.

Honestly… I thought I knew her well. We talked for years—over coffee, at rallies, sitting on that same garden bench where we used to split an empanada. But doing this today—speaking *as* her, not just *about* her—I felt something shift.

I realized… she didn’t just *have* opinions. She carried them like scars and stitches. Every word was tied to a face, a name, a memory. It wasn’t abstract. It was personal. Like when she talked about refugees—she wasn’t thinking of “policy.” She was seeing her cousin’s boy, the one who disappeared for six months during the gang sweeps in Soyapango. That changed how I hear the word “border” now. It’s not a line on a map. It’s someone’s child walking it barefoot.

And I’ll admit—I’ve been more afraid than I let on. Afraid that if we keep letting people in, there won’t be enough. For my son. For his future. But stepping into her shoes today… I saw how small that fear looks next to her hope. Her stubborn belief that community isn’t something you’re born into—it’s something you build, brick by brick, with people you didn’t choose.

She never dismissed the struggles of locals. Never said, “Just deal with it.” But she also refused to see newcomers as threats. To her, both were caught in the same broken system. And instead of choosing sides, she wanted to fix the game.

That’s what moved me most—her refusal to hate. Even when she was tired. Even when she was scared.

Doing this… it didn’t change my mind so much as deepen it. Like roots going further down. I still worry about jobs, about strain on schools, about safety. But now I carry her question with me: *“Are we solving the real problem—or just punishing the wrong people?”*

And I realize—honoring her isn’t just remembering her laugh or how she always brought extra tortillas. It’s living like she did. With open eyes. A guarded heart, maybe—but one willing to stretch.

So thank you. Not just for inviting me to speak as her. For giving me a chance to *listen* to her again. Because today, I didn’t just play a role.  
I remembered a friend.  
And I found my way back to hope.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character43_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Okay, let me sit in her skin a minute.

Fairness, for me, was never just laws on paper. It’s how those laws land on people who have to punch a clock and still come home to cook and help with homework. Fairness means clear rules that apply the same whether you have a lawyer on speed dial or you’re figuring it out after a ten-hour shift. I used to say, “Don’t make it a maze for the poor and a fast lane for the rich.” If you work, you should be paid what was promised, on time, no games. If you pay into the pot, you should have a right to basic protections—seeing a doctor, feeling safe calling the police when you’re a victim, your kids getting a fair shot at school. And fairness has mercy in it: people make mistakes, life pushes you—there should be a way to fix your status, to correct things without living with a target on your back forever. But yes, I also believed in responsibility: show up, follow the rules you agree to, don’t cut corners that put others at risk.

Belonging… that one sits in my chest. Belonging is two-sided. You earn it by showing up, learning how things are done here, respecting your neighbors. And it’s offered when others look at you—with your accent, your lunch that smells different, your kids who are learning two languages—and still say, “You’re one of us.” I’ve felt both doors: the teacher who asked me to speak about El Salvador at career day—that made me feel seen—and the lady at the grocery who told me to “go back.” Belonging for me is making pupusas for the school fundraiser, cheering at the soccer field, and also being invited to sit on the PTA, not just asked to bring plates. It’s layered: I’m Salvadoreña in my bones, and I’m also from this city because I’ve watered its plants, paid its taxes, learned its weather and its people.

Community is practical. It’s who holds your spare key, who watches your kids when your bus is late, who brings caldo when you’re sick. In our building, we had a little WhatsApp—rides to the clinic, extra pan dulce after church, a heads-up if someone sketchy was hanging around. Community doesn’t mean we all agree; it means we argue without trying to break each other. We don’t call the cops first—we knock on the door, we talk. We make a sign-up for the community garden. We put a box by the mailroom for school supplies in August so no one has to ask. My rule was, “Nos cuidamos—we take care of each other.” That includes the new family on the third floor and the old man who’s been there thirty years.

Some moments that shaped me: translating at the clinic for a neighbor because the nurse was rushing her and she looked scared. Sitting in a union hall learning my rights after a boss tried to shave our hours. The first time my daughter corrected my English, and the pride and sting of that. Getting a text from a neighbor, “We saved you a plate,” after a long day. Those are my definitions—fairness, belonging, community—built from the kitchen table up, not from a podium.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character43_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting there with dirt under my nails, I hear three, four languages at once—kids kicking a ball, an abuela humming, someone FaceTiming their mom back home—and honestly, it makes me feel calm. That mix feels like my life: a little homesick, a little proud, very busy, but together.

I like meeting people through doing, not speeches. Passing someone the watering can, asking how their cilantro’s doing, sharing a bag of limes—those little exchanges open the door. Food is the bridge I trust most. I bring pupusas, they bring samosas or dumplings, and suddenly we’re telling stories about our grandmothers. I try to learn names, at least one word in their language, and something about their day that isn’t just weather.

Do I ever feel awkward? Sure. Sometimes I don’t get a joke, or I worry I’ll step on a custom I don’t know. Sometimes folks keep to themselves because they’ve been burned or they’re tired, and I get that. I lead with patience and a smile, and I don’t push. You show up consistently—return the Tupperware, keep the hose rolled, stick to quiet hours—and trust grows.

I’m also practical about boundaries. I can be friendly and still say, “Hey, the gate needs to stay closed so the little ones don’t run out,” or “Let’s keep the music lower after nine.” Identity is never the problem; behavior in shared spaces is what we work on together. If there’s a misunderstanding, I knock and talk before making it a big deal. And I share the load—translating when I can, but also encouraging others to help so it doesn’t fall on the same few people.

Mostly, I feel grateful. Every person brings a piece—recipes, songs, skills, stories. When we make room for that, the garden grows better, and so do we.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
I always came back to two words: respeto and claridad. Respect and clear expectations. People live different lives, but we share the same space, so we set simple, fair rules that focus on behavior, not identity, and we write them big, in plain language, in more than one language.

What helps everyone feel comfortable:
- Clear, posted norms: quiet hours, clean-up after yourself, keep paths clear, close the gate so kids don’t run out, no slurs or harassment—ever. Same rules for everybody, no exceptions for “regulars” or for folks with money.
- Multilingual and visual: signs in Spanish/English (and others if we can), pictures for key rules, and a buddy system so new neighbors aren’t lost.
- Small, steady gestures: learn names, pronouns if people share them, share food without making it a test, and keep invitations open—“bring your partner/family/friend,” no assumptions.
- Privacy as a baseline: we don’t gossip about health, papers, or people’s pasts. If someone shares, we treat it with care.

On specific situations:

Alcohol or substance struggles:
- We judge behavior, not people. If someone is intoxicated in the garden, we check they’re safe, offer water and a seat, and make sure tools are put away so no one gets hurt.
- We set boundaries: no using in shared family spaces, no open containers around kids, and keep glass out.
- We keep resource cards handy for support services. Some neighbors choose to get trained on overdose response and keep naloxone; that’s about saving lives, not shaming. If there’s immediate danger, we call for help.

Infectious diseases:
- We don’t ask folks about diagnoses. We use universal care: wash hands, don’t share cups or cigarettes, wipe down shared tools, cover cuts, stay home if you’re actively sick.
- Masks are always okay—no comments. We follow public health guidance if there’s an outbreak.
- We make it easy to be safe: hand gel by the hose, paper towels, labeled bins.

Different racial, religious, linguistic backgrounds:
- We meet people where they are—slow down our speech, use translation apps, build a volunteer list of bilingual neighbors so the same person isn’t translating every time.
- We celebrate without putting anyone on display. If someone offers to share a tradition, we make space; we don’t demand it.
- If there’s a careless comment, we correct gently but firmly: “We don’t talk about people like that here.”

LGBTQ+ neighbors, unmarried couples, different family shapes:
- Treat every family the same. No intrusive questions about relationships or bodies. If someone shares their pronouns, we use them; if they don’t, we don’t force it.
- Our code of conduct covers slurs and harassment. First a private reminder, then mediation if needed.

Where we need extra communication and tolerance:
- Noise and celebrations: people mark holidays differently. We set quiet hours with room for occasional events if neighbors are notified. Put big gatherings on a shared calendar.
- Smells—food, incense, smoke: we can designate smoke-free zones and times, and talk about ventilation instead of shaming traditions.
- Kids and safety: agree on basic supervision, tool storage, and locked gates. Many hands prevent accidents.
- Pets: leashes, cleanup, and a plan for dogs who are nervous around kids.

Why this matters:
- People carry shame around addiction, fear around illness, trauma from past discrimination, or worry about police and immigration. Clear, fair rules and a culture of “ask first, assume good intent” lower the temperature so folks aren’t defensive.
- Consistency builds trust. If the rules are the same for the pastor’s wife, the young guys who just moved in, and the old timer on the corner, people relax.

How we handle problems:
- Step 1: friendly check-in—“Hey neighbor, can we talk about the music after nine?”
- Step 2: bring a neutral buddy if it’s awkward.
- Step 3: short group check-in at the garden once a month to adjust what’s not working.
- Step 4: if someone’s safety is at risk, we act fast and call the right help.

My bottom line: we don’t need everyone to be the same; we need the space to be safe enough for differences. Nos cuidamos—we take care of each other—with warm hearts and firm boundaries. That’s how people breathe easier and keep coming back.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character43_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
When jobs are tight, fairness to me starts with not letting bosses turn neighbors into rivals. The easiest way to pit people against each other is to make one group cheaper and quieter to exploit. So I always said: set the same floor for everyone and enforce it. If the floor is solid, the race to the bottom slows down.

What fairness looks like:
- Same pay for the same work, same safety rules, same overtime—no matter where you were born or what papers you have. That takes away the incentive to hire someone just because you can underpay them.
- Go after wage theft and shady contractors hard. Most of the harm I’ve seen comes from companies shaving hours, misclassifying people as “independent,” or bringing in temps to dodge benefits. Hit that, and you protect both the guy laid off last month and the woman who crossed a border to feed her kids.
- Real pathways that match real jobs. If a sector truly can’t find people—farm work, elder care, certain trades—make legal visas that require prevailing wages, decent housing when needed, and the right to change employers so people aren’t trapped. If unemployment rises, you dial those numbers down; when it falls, you open them up—but you never play with humanitarian cases like they’re a faucet.
- Invest in local workers so they can actually qualify: apprenticeships, ESL tied to job training, childcare during classes, help recognizing foreign credentials, bus passes to get to worksites. On city-funded projects, give local applicants first shot and do outreach in multiple languages. That’s not a wall; it’s a ramp.
- Hiring halls and posted rates for day labor so it’s not a scramble on the corner where the lowest bid wins. You put up the daily rate, the safety rules, and everyone signs in—less chaos, less undercutting.
- Strong unions or worker committees that include everyone. When we bargained as a mixed crew, wages went up for all. When people are scared to speak because of status, everybody’s pay slips.
- Target enforcement at employers, not raids that tear apart families. If you use systems to check work authorization, pair them with fast ways to fix status errors and with anti-discrimination guardrails, so people aren’t punished for their last name.

Balancing locals and migrants, I think in layers:
- Roots matter. People who’ve lived here, paid taxes, and lost a job in a plant closing shouldn’t be invisible. So on public contracts or big incentives, require local hiring goals and training slots. That helps the guy down the block see a path back in.
- Dignity matters. Migrant workers are often filling roles others don’t take at the wages offered or in seasons locals can’t cover. If we protect them from being used as a cheap lever, resentment cools, and more locals consider those jobs when the pay and conditions improve.
- Community capacity matters. If a neighborhood absorbs new workers, tie funding to that—schools, clinics, transit—so people don’t feel like they’re competing for a doctor’s appointment or a seat in kindergarten.

Why I feel this way: I’ve sat in the union hall learning how my boss skimmed our time. I’ve translated for a roofer who broke his wrist and was scared to file a claim. The problem wasn’t my neighbor from Oaxaca; it was the contractor cutting corners. When the city set up an apprenticeship on a public works job—with outreach in Spanish and English and a small stipend for childcare—my cousin got in, and so did two recent arrivals. Pay held steady, no one undercut, and everyone went home safer.

So, balance to me is not “locals first, everyone else last.” It’s “rules first, dignity for all,” with smart knobs you can turn when the economy tightens. You lift the floor, you build ramps for locals to step up, and you stop the games that make us glare at each other across the break room. That’s how we share scarce jobs without tearing the community.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character43_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
I’ve heard all those arguments at barbecues, on the bus, in union meetings. I sort them into three piles: what matches both lived life and the data, what’s a real pain point we can fix with policy, and what’s mostly fear that needs facts and calmer talk.

- Immigrants fill vital roles/labor shortages: That rings true. In my world it’s fields, kitchens, roofs, elder care, meatpacking, housekeeping, some trades—jobs that are hard, seasonal, or at hours locals can’t or won’t cover at the pay offered. But the fix isn’t “import cheap labor forever.” It’s set and enforce real labor standards, create legal, flexible visas tied to prevailing wages and the right to switch employers, and train local workers alongside newcomers. If a sector can’t find people at a fair wage even after that, then yes, targeted immigration makes sense.

- Cultural diversity and vitality: I feel that in my bones. New food, languages, music—that’s life-giving. But culture can’t be a substitute for fairness. People won’t celebrate your pupusas if they think you’re taking their shift. So we pair the “festival” with the “floor”: celebrate differences while building shared norms—English learning plus pride in home language, civic classes, and chances to work together on something practical.

- Security concerns—crime, social tensions, terrorism: Wanting safety is reasonable. What I’ve seen and what most studies say is immigrants overall aren’t more likely to commit crimes than folks born here, and sometimes less when you account for age and poverty. The crime I’ve most run into is against immigrants—wage theft, exploitation, trafficking. So we focus police on serious violence and the exploiters, and we build trust so victims aren’t scared to report. On terrorism, refugees and many visa holders go through heavy vetting already; the risk isn’t zero, but it’s low and better managed by good intelligence than by painting whole groups as dangerous. Social tensions are real when schools, clinics, or housing are stretched. That’s not a reason to slam the door; it’s a reason to send resources where people are settling and to do better planning and communication.

- Humanitarian arguments: I’m from a place where people run because staying can mean death or hunger. A country with our size should keep a firm, orderly door for refugees and people with real asylum claims—fair hearings, quicker decisions, and support to get on their feet. That’s not charity; many of those families stabilize neighborhoods and pay back in taxes and service.

- Impact on jobs and income: This is where fear lives. Big-picture, the overall effect on wages is small, but it can bite in specific places—low-wage sectors, towns hit by plant closures. Blaming the woman from Guatemala is easy; the real levers are employers who underpay, temp schemes, and weak enforcement. Level the floor—same pay for same work, hit wage theft hard, support unions—and the “they’re taking our jobs” heat drops. Also, invest in on-ramps: apprenticeships, ESL tied to trades, childcare during training, and recognition of foreign skills. And if the economy tightens, adjust work visa numbers transparently instead of lurching.

What feels reasonable to me:
- Yes, immigrants can relieve shortages and add energy—reasonable.
- Yes, communities need support when populations grow—reasonable.
- Yes, we must take security seriously—reasonable, but focus on facts and targeted enforcement.
- Yes, some workers can feel squeezed—reasonable; answer it with stronger labor standards and training, not scapegoats.
- The idea that immigrants drive crime or terrorism as a group—needs more facts; most evidence doesn’t back that broad claim.
- The idea that culture alone justifies policy—thin. Policy must rest on fairness, capacity, and clear rules.

What I’d like more evidence and dialogue on:
- Local, not just national, data: wages and rents before/after big influxes, school capacity, clinic wait times—so we can target help.
- Independent audits of visa programs: are they meeting real shortages at fair wages, or being used to undercut?
- How fast asylum and work permit systems can move without sacrificing due process—long limbo helps no one.
- What mix of integration supports (language classes, credential recognition, mental health for trauma) gives the best outcomes for both newcomers and longtime residents.

My bottom line stays the same: rules with a heart. Set one fair floor for work, invest where people settle, keep a steady, vetted humanitarian lane, and give communities a say and the resources to manage change. Do that, and a lot of the fear turns down, and we can talk to each other like neighbors again.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character43_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I never liked the extremes. “Let everyone in” sounds kind until you get to the school office and the clinic line, and “shut it down” sounds strong until you meet the roofer who’s keeping your block dry. I want rules with a heart—order that doesn’t turn people into leverage.

The mix I’d back:

- A steady humanitarian lane:
  - Keep a firm, well-resourced path for refugees and people with real asylum claims—quick, fair decisions, work authorization while they wait, and support to settle. That’s about dignity and order at the same time.

- Demand-based work visas with worker protections:
  - Tie visas to real shortages, proven with transparent data and input from unions and local boards.
  - Require prevailing wages, safe conditions, and portability—the right to change employers—so no one is trapped and undercutting can’t be the business model.
  - Build in training slots for local workers alongside newcomers—apprenticeships, ESL linked to trades, childcare during classes.

- Numerical limits that adjust with the economy:
  - Set category caps (seasonal, care work, skilled trades) that rise or fall based on unemployment and vacancy rates. Publish the numbers and the reasons so people see the knobs, not just the results.
  - Spread arrivals so one neighborhood isn’t overwhelmed; send funding with people—schools, clinics, transit.

- Family unity:
  - Keep a clear path for immediate family to reunite, with reasonable timelines. Stable families make stable workers and neighbors.

- Earned stabilization for those already woven into communities:
  - If someone’s been here years, paying taxes, with no serious crimes, give a way to fix status—fees, background checks, civics and language classes. Shadows are where exploitation grows.

- Focus enforcement on employers, not fear:
  - Hit wage theft and abusive contractors hard. Pair any work authorization checks with fast fixes for errors and anti-discrimination guardrails.

- Border and processing that are humane and orderly:
  - More legal entry points and appointments, alternatives to detention for families, and quicker, consistent decisions. Chaos helps smugglers, not communities.

Why this balance:
- It keeps bosses from playing us against each other. Same floor, same rights—less incentive to hire the most vulnerable just to squeeze costs.
- It answers real needs—harvests, elder care, rebuilding roofs—without pretending cheap labor is the only way.
- It gives neighborhoods breathing room and resources so belonging isn’t a slogan; it’s a full classroom and a clinic with appointments.
- It respects the woman running from danger and the man laid off from the plant. Both deserve a fair shot and a clear path.

Complete openness ignores capacity and invites exploitation. A hard “no” shuts out families and sectors that truly need hands. Demand-based with adjustable numbers, a protected humanitarian lane, and strong labor standards—that’s where fairness and integration meet. Set one fair floor, build ramps for locals and newcomers to step up, and stop the games. That’s how we keep the community garden—and the country—growing without tearing the roots.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character43_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character43_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
I did. Slipping into her voice reminded me how much of her “politics” came from the kitchen table and the job site, not from headlines. A few things clicked sharper:

- Fairness, to her, was floors not walls—clear rules that apply to everyone, with a little mercy built in. And it was always about behavior, not identity. I felt how that plays out from the garden gate to the hiring hall.
- Belonging is two‑sided. You show up and learn the ropes, and your neighbors meet you halfway. I could feel how small rituals—returning a Tupperware, learning a name, a note on the bulletin board—do more work than any speech.
- Community is practical tenderness: warm hearts, firm boundaries. That phrase kept coming back to me when thinking about addiction, illness, or just noise at night.
- At the policy level, she didn’t live on slogans. She trusted dials over switches: a steady humanitarian lane, work visas tied to real shortages with portability and prevailing wages, numerical caps that move with the economy, family unity, earned stabilization for people already woven in, and enforcement aimed at exploiters. It’s a toolkit, not a single hammer.

About her, I remembered why people listened to her even when they didn’t agree: she could hold two truths at once—capacity matters and dignity matters—and keep the focus on rules that stop us from being played against each other.

For me, it nudged some things:
- I’m less tempted by the comfort of extremes. “Open everything” and “close everything” both skip the hard work she cared about.
- I’m more convinced that labor standards and employer enforcement are the pressure points if you want to cool resentment and lift wages.
- I see more clearly that communities need resources with arrivals—schools, clinics, transit—or else even good policy feels bad on the ground.
- I’m firmer on having a real, protected humanitarian path and on creating a way out of the shadows for long‑time neighbors who are contributing.
- And it made me look at my own habits: show up more, translate without hoarding the job, push for apprenticeships with childcare, help set the norms in shared spaces.

Channeling her didn’t change my basic values, but it grounded them. It made the balance—rules with a heart—feel less like a line and more like a practice, from the garden up to the national level. And it made me miss her steadiness; she had a way of turning heat into light.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character43_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Of course. Speaking as Character43_F, I’d say that fairness is really about everyone getting an equal chance, no matter where you come from or what you look like. Growing up in a working-class Hispanic family, I saw a lot of people judged or left out just because they spoke with an accent or didn’t have the right papers. That never felt right to me. Fairness means no one’s treated as less than—everyone deserves respect and the chance to work for a better life.

When it comes to belonging, it’s deeply personal. There’s something about walking into a room and not having to explain yourself—whether that’s your background, your family, or why you celebrate certain holidays. I always believed in finding ways to make people feel welcome, especially those who felt like outsiders. I remember how hard it was for my mom when she first came to the US, always feeling like she was on the edge of things. That’s why I care so much about inclusion.

Community, to me, is people looking out for each other. In our neighborhood, we didn’t have much, but we shared what we had. People helped each other—whether it was lending a hand with childcare, passing down clothes, or just listening when someone needed it. Real community is about trust, mutual respect, and showing up for each other, especially when times are tough.

What stands out most to me are those little moments: someone translating for a neighbor at the clinic, folks sharing food at the church festival, or people rallying together when someone lost their job. That’s what I think of when I talk about fairness, belonging, and community.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character43_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting here in the community garden, seeing all sorts of faces—different colors, accents, ways of dressing—it honestly makes me feel proud of our neighborhood. I like that you can hear Spanish, English, sometimes even other languages just walking down the block. It reminds me of how my own family was welcomed, how we found a little corner where we could be ourselves and still be part of something bigger.

When it comes to interacting with neighbors, I usually feel curious and open. I know what it’s like to be treated as “other,” so I try not to judge anyone for being different. Sometimes it’s a little awkward at first, especially if you don’t know if you’ll understand each other, but I’ve learned that a smile and a little patience go a long way.

Now, I’m not going to pretend everything is always easy. There are people who struggle more—maybe with addiction, mental health, or just getting by. Some situations can make you nervous, but I believe it’s important to treat people with respect and at least give them a chance. I try to remember that everyone’s got their story, and a lot of us have faced tough times one way or another.

Honestly, I think the diversity makes our community stronger. We’re not perfect—sometimes there are misunderstandings, and sometimes people need to talk things through. But I’d rather live in a place where people are different and learning from each other than somewhere everyone is the same and shut off. I always hope we can keep building those bridges, little by little.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
I think that, for me, making everyone comfortable starts with being real and respectful. You don’t have to pretend you understand everyone’s life, but you can show kindness and not judge. I’ve seen a lot in my own neighborhood—people fighting addiction, families not looking “traditional,” folks having to deal with health problems, and all kinds of backgrounds mixed together. What’s important is not turning away, even when you don’t get it. Just letting people know they belong here, too.

Sometimes I notice people keep their distance from neighbors who struggle with alcoholism or drug use, almost like they’re afraid or just don’t want to get involved. I get it—sometimes you have to protect yourself or your kids. But ignoring people or acting like they’re invisible only makes things worse. I think small gestures matter—a “good morning,” offering help if someone seems in trouble, or even just not gossiping about them can go a long way. There’s times when you need clear boundaries, but there’s always a way to be humane.

For folks with infectious diseases or who need special care, honestly, I think there’s a lot of misunderstanding. People get scared and start rumors. That’s when communication is really important—sometimes just learning the facts and talking openly can make things less scary for everyone. I remember when there was a case of tuberculosis in our building, and people panicked. But after someone from the clinic explained how it worked and how to stay safe, things calmed down and people were able to help each other.

Religion and language differences—you see that every day. I’ve always felt that food and celebrations are the easiest way to bring people together. But I've met several such families now through my children's school, and I can see they love their children just as much as I love mine. I might not understand everything about their lives, but I respect their right to live them.

What makes everyone comfortable? Clear communication, respect for boundaries, and finding common ground—usually our children or our work experiences. When misunderstandings happen, we need to talk directly but kindly. Like when the new family from Somalia moved in and their children were playing loudly very late at night. Instead of complaining, I brought them coffee and explained our neighborhood's unspoken rules. They weren't being disrespectful; they just didn't know.

The situations needing more tolerance are usually when our cultural or religious differences seem to clash. But I've found that when we focus on our shared humanity—we all want safe neighborhoods, good schools, and opportunities for our children—those differences become less important.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character43_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*speaking as Character43_F*

This hits close to home for me. I remember when I first came here, taking whatever jobs I could find—cleaning houses, working night shifts at a factory, all while trying to improve my English and get my certification. Some people looked at me like I was stealing their opportunities, but I was just trying to feed my family like everyone else.

Fairness... it's complicated when resources are tight. I believe everyone who works hard deserves a chance, but I also understand the frustration when it feels like there aren't enough jobs to go around.

First, I think fairness means legal pathways. I came legally, waited my turn, filled out mountains of paperwork, paid fees I could barely afford. It wasn't easy, but I did it right. It's not fair when others skip that process. But the system is broken too—it takes too long, costs too much. Many good people can't wait years when their families are hungry now.

Second, fairness means equal pay for equal work. I've seen too many employers hire immigrants because they can pay them less or make them work in unsafe conditions. That hurts everyone—it undercuts wages for locals and exploits vulnerable people who can't complain. If everyone had to follow the same labor laws and pay the same wages, much of this tension would disappear.

Third, I think communities need to invest in training for jobs that are actually available. When I got my technical certification in medical billing, it opened doors that weren't there before. Both locals and immigrants need these pathways to better jobs.

As for balance, I believe in prioritizing people already here legally—citizens and legal residents—for government assistance programs and certain job training opportunities. That seems fair to me. But I also think we need temporary worker programs that allow people to come legally for jobs that truly need filling, especially in agriculture and construction. My cousin works seasonal farm jobs in California, and those farmers can't find enough local workers willing to do that difficult work.

The problem isn't really immigrants versus locals. It's that our economy doesn't create enough good jobs for everyone. When companies move factories overseas but executives get huge bonuses, that's what's unfair. We're fighting over crumbs while others take the whole cake.

In my community, I've seen how we can work together when we stop blaming each other. The local community college started offering evening English classes and technical training, and now both immigrants and locals are getting better jobs. That's the kind of solution we need more of.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character43_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*speaking as Character43_F*

When I hear these national debates about immigration, I often think how different they sound from my lived experience. Let me break down how I see these different perspectives.

On immigrants filling vital roles—this is absolutely true in my experience. In the hospital where I work in billing, we have doctors from India, nurses from the Philippines, and custodial staff from all over Latin America. Without them, healthcare in this country would collapse. Same with agriculture—I have family members who pick crops that would rot in fields without immigrant labor. These aren't just opinions; these are facts I see with my own eyes.

About cultural diversity being valuable—I see this in my children's lives. They speak two languages fluently, understand different perspectives, and can navigate different cultural expectations. That's an advantage in today's world. But I also understand when communities worry about changing too fast. Integration takes time and effort from both sides.

Now, regarding security concerns—this is where I think we need more honest conversation backed by real data. Are there bad people who immigrate? Of course, just like there are bad people born here. But the vast majority of immigrants I know are extremely law-abiding because we can't afford not to be. One mistake could mean deportation. The fear of immigrants bringing crime often seems much larger than the reality.

For terrorism specifically—that requires serious security screening, which I support. I went through extensive background checks to come here legally. But painting all immigrants, especially those from certain countries or religions, as potential threats? That's unfair and creates more division.

The humanitarian perspective resonates deeply with me. I came for economic opportunity, but I have friends who fled genuine danger—political persecution, gang violence, domestic abuse. Their stories would break your heart. Offering refuge to those truly in need reflects the best of American values.

On economic impacts—this is complicated. In some industries, an influx of willing workers can depress wages. That's just supply and demand. But immigrants are also consumers who create demand for housing, food, services—which creates jobs. And many start businesses—like my brother-in-law's construction company that now employs twelve people, including six who were born here.

What viewpoints seem reasonable? I think concerns about illegal immigration undermining legal pathways are valid. I think recognizing the economic contributions of immigrants is factual. I think humanitarian concerns for refugees are moral. And I think wanting secure borders is reasonable—every country has that right.

What needs more evidence? The claims that immigrants are primarily responsible for crime, that they're a net drain on public resources, or that they don't want to integrate. My experience and the research I've seen contradicts these claims, but I'm open to honest conversation backed by real facts.

What frustrates me most about this national debate is how it ignores the complex realities of real people's lives. Immigration isn't just a policy issue—it's about families, communities, and shared futures. We need to talk to each other, not just about each other.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character43_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*speaking as Character43_F*

I've thought about this a lot, especially watching how policies have affected my own family and community over the years. Let me be clear—I don't support either extreme. Complete openness without any controls would overwhelm our systems and communities. But completely closing borders is neither realistic nor humane.

For me, the best approach would be a combination—admitting people primarily based on job demand, with reasonable numerical limits, plus a separate humanitarian pathway for refugees and asylum seekers.

First, we need a functional guest worker program. The current system is broken. When I see agricultural workers or construction crews working without proper documentation, it's not because they want to break laws—it's because there's no realistic legal path for them. Employers need these workers, workers need these jobs, so let's create a legal, regulated system that protects both sides. These temporary visas should be tied to actual job offers, with labor protections to prevent exploitation.

Second, we need to maintain and improve our skills-based immigration system. This would include both highly educated professionals like doctors and engineers, but also skilled trades that we need—like experienced construction workers, healthcare aides, or chefs. My certification in medical billing helped me contribute more to this country's economy, and that path should be available to others.

Third, we need reasonable numerical limits that can adjust based on economic conditions. When the economy is booming and jobs are plentiful, we can welcome more people. During recessions, those numbers might need to decrease. This isn't about race or country of origin—it should be about our capacity to integrate newcomers successfully.

Fourth, we absolutely need a separate, efficient humanitarian system. People fleeing persecution or disaster need a different process than economic migrants. I know families who waited years in dangerous conditions for their asylum cases to be heard. That's not right. We can be both orderly and compassionate.

What about fairness and integration? Fairness means clear rules that are actually enforced, waiting your turn, and contributing to your new country through work and taxes. But fairness also means creating enough legal pathways that match reality. It's not fair to have a system so broken that it practically forces people to go around it.

For integration, I believe in both rights and responsibilities. Immigrants should have access to language classes, job training, and community support. But they also have a responsibility to learn English, understand American laws and customs, and participate in their communities. My church offers English classes, and I volunteer there because I know how important language is for success here.

Finally, we need to address the root causes of migration in countries like mine. Foreign policy and economic development that creates opportunities in other countries means fewer people feel forced to leave home. I love the United States, but I would have preferred to stay in El Salvador if I could have supported my family there.

This balanced approach isn't as simple as open or closed borders. It requires ongoing adjustment and honest conversation. But it's the only way forward that respects both our national interests and our humanity.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character43_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
*settling into the conversation, speaking as Character43_F*

You know, fairness to me has always been about everyone getting a real shot, not just the people who already have connections or came from money. Growing up Hispanic in this country, I've seen how some folks get opportunities handed to them while others - people just as hardworking, just as deserving - have to fight twice as hard for half as much. That's not right.

When I think about belonging, it's complicated. I've always felt caught between worlds sometimes - not quite fitting into certain spaces because of my background, but also knowing this is my home. Belonging isn't just about being tolerated; it's about being valued for what you bring to the table. It's about people seeing you as part of the fabric of the community, not just someone passing through.

And community... *pauses thoughtfully* Community is everything. It's the people who show up when your car breaks down and you can't afford the repair shop. It's the neighbors who watch each other's kids, who share resources when times are tough. But real community requires trust, and trust takes time to build. It needs people who are invested in staying, in making things better together.

I've always believed that fairness means we look out for the people who are already here struggling - the working families trying to make ends meet, the kids in our schools who need more support. That has to come first before we can extend that same care to others.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character43_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*looking around the garden, watching different neighbors tending their plots*

I've gotten to know Mrs. Chen who grows the most incredible vegetables - she's taught me things about companion planting I never knew. And there's Miguel who always shares his tomatoes when he has extras. These are good people, hardworking people who care about this place.

But I'll be honest - it takes time to build those connections. Sometimes there are language barriers, or different ways of doing things that can cause little tensions. Like when some folks weren't following the watering schedule we all agreed on, or when cultural differences meant different ideas about how to handle conflicts.

What I've learned is that the people who really become part of the community are the ones who make an effort to understand how things work here, who contribute to making it better for everyone. It's not about changing who you are, but about finding ways to fit into the rhythm we've all created together.

The diversity can be beautiful - I mean, look at all these different vegetables and herbs growing side by side. But it works because we all follow the same basic rules, we all put in the work, and we all want the same thing: a little piece of something good we can call our own.

When someone's struggling but they're still trying to be a good neighbor, people will rally around them. We need more honest conversations, not walking on eggshells, but real talk about how we can all live together safely.

Fairness to me means we take care of our own first. I'm not talking about being cruel to anyone, but when there aren't enough good jobs to go around, shouldn't the people who've been contributing to this community, paying taxes here, sending their kids to school here - shouldn't they get first shot at opportunities?

*voice getting more passionate*

And here's the thing - I'm Hispanic, my family came here looking for better opportunities too. But there's a difference between coming here legally, learning the system, becoming part of the community versus just showing up and taking whatever work you can get under the table.

I think we need policies that protect workers who are already here - all workers, not just certain groups. If companies want to hire from outside the community, they should have to prove they couldn't find local people to do the job, and they should have to pay the same wages they'd pay anyone else.

It's not about being against immigrants. It's about making sure working families aren't thrown under the bus.

responses.answer:

You know, I can see truth in several of these perspectives, and that's what makes this so complicated.

The labor shortage argument - yeah, I get it. There are jobs Americans don't want to do, especially for the wages being offered. But here's my question: maybe if those jobs paid better, had decent benefits, treated workers with respect, more Americans would want them? When I hear "jobs Americans won't do," sometimes I think it really means "jobs that don't pay enough for Americans to live on."

The cultural diversity piece... look, I appreciate good food, music, different traditions. My own culture adds to this country. But diversity works best when it happens gradually, when communities have time to adjust and integrate. When it's too fast, too much at once, that's when you get the tensions and resentment.

*pauses, voice becoming more serious*

The security concerns - I won't lie, they worry me. Not because I think all immigrants are dangerous, but because I've seen what happens in my neighborhood when systems get overwhelmed. When there aren't enough resources for proper screening, when agencies are stretched too thin, when people are living in the shadows - that creates problems for everyone.

The humanitarian argument touches my heart. My own family fled poverty and violence. But we also have homeless veterans on our streets, kids in our schools who don't have enough to eat. How do we help people abroad when we're not taking care of people here?

*leans back*

What I need to see is real data - not just emotional appeals from either side. Show me the actual numbers on wages, crime rates, costs to communities. And most importantly, show me plans that don't leave working families like mine worse off than before.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character43_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*sits back, considering each option carefully*

Complete openness? That's just not realistic. I mean, think about it - if everyone who wanted to come could just show up, what happens to wages? What happens to housing costs? What happens to our schools and hospitals that are already stretched thin? My heart goes out to people who want better lives, but we can't help anyone if we overwhelm our own systems.

Refusing entry completely - that's not right either. This country was built by immigrants, including my own family. We'd be hypocrites to slam the door shut now.

*leans forward, speaking more decisively*

I think the smartest approach is a combination - job-based immigration with numerical limits that make sense for what our communities can actually handle.

Here's how I'd want it to work: First, prove there's a real labor shortage that can't be filled by people already here - and I mean at wages that people can actually live on. If McDonald's can't find workers at $7 an hour, maybe the problem isn't worker shortage, maybe it's the wage.

Second, set limits based on what local communities can absorb. Some places might be able to handle more newcomers, others are already struggling. Let local people have a say in what their communities can manage.

Third, prioritize people who are coming here to build something, not just take whatever they can get. People who want to learn English, who want to become citizens, who want their kids to be Americans.

*voice becoming more emphatic*

And here's the key - anyone who comes here legally should get the same labor protections as everyone else. No undercutting wages, no exploiting people because they're desperate. That protects everyone - the newcomers and the people already here.

It's about being smart and fair, not just emotional.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character43_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Fairness? To her, it was never some far-off idea in books or laws. It was real—like when she’d tell me, “You know, J, fairness is when you get a shot. Not special treatment, not handouts—but a real chance to work hard and make something, same as anybody else.” She’d say this with fire, like it wasn’t just about policy, but dignity.

She grew up watching both her parents work two jobs—her mom cleaning offices, her dad driving a delivery van. They weren’t asking for pity, just respect. That shaped her. Fairness meant people shouldn’t be punished for where they started. Especially if they’re willing to roll up their sleeves.

Belonging… that one cut deep for her. Being US-Hispanic in El Salvador—she didn’t always feel seen. Not fully from here, not quite fitting back “home” either, even though her family roots were Salvadoran. She once told me, “I’m not foreign, but sometimes I feel like one.” She carried that quietly. But because of it, she had this soft spot for anyone who felt on the edge of a circle—like they were peering in but not invited in.

Community, to her, wasn’t just geography. It was *who shows up*. Like when old Mr. Ruiz fell sick and couldn’t pay his meds—she organized a collection at the bus depot where she worked part-time. People chipped in cash, others brought food. That’s what community meant: looking out. Not waiting for the government. Doing it together.

She used to say, “A community isn’t strong because everyone’s the same. It’s strong when different people choose to care for each other anyway.” And she lived that. Even when it was hard. Especially then.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character43_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*sitting back slightly, hands resting on knees, voice calm but firm*

You know, when I sit here in the garden, pulling weeds or just watching the sun hit the marigolds, I see all kinds of people. Maria from Guatemala, always bringing extra tamales even though her back hurts from cleaning houses all day. The young Somali couple with the baby—so quiet, so careful, like they’re afraid to take up space. And then there’s Mr. Bell, veteran, sleeps rough sometimes under the awning at the laundromat, smells like whiskey but never harms nobody.

I don’t look at them and think, *Oh, what a problem.* I think, *We’re all trying.* Some of us are broken in different ways. Some of us came from war, some from poverty, some just from bad choices. But we’re all here now. Sharing this dirt, these tomatoes, this air.

I remember one time, that transgender girl—Lena, she’s Puerto Rican and Black—was planting kale, and someone left a note on her plot: “This ain’t for freaks.” She almost left. But me and three others—we replanted her bed together, put up a little sign that said, *All Roots Welcome.* Took her weeks, but she smiled again. That’s what matters.

I won’t lie—I get nervous sometimes. When someone’s high and talking to themselves near the kids, yeah, my stomach tightens. Or when the landlord brings in new renters with no furniture, clearly asylum seekers or whatever, and the city doesn’t help, just dumps them here like we’ve got infinite room. Then the water’s overused, trash piles up… that’s not fair to the rest of us either.

But still. I believe in giving people a chance to belong. Not because they’re perfect—but because *we* aren’t either. My tía used to say, “La caridad empieza en casa, pero no termina ahí.” Charity starts at home, but it don’t end there.

So I’ll keep saying hello. Keep offering seeds. Keep asking, “You okay?” Even if the answer’s silence. Because that’s how trust grows. Like beans on a trellis—one tendril at a time.

Look… I was raised Catholic. My mom still crosses herself when she hears certain words. Not because I’m bad, but because that wasn’t what I was taught.

But then I watched them. How James stayed up all night with her when she had the croup. How Eli fixed Mrs. Gutierrez’s step without asking for anything. And I thought: *What kind of person am I if love like that scares me?* So I leaned into the discomfort. Asked questions. Listened. Took my time.

That’s how it should be—with everything. With the man who drinks too much down by the fence line, with the woman from Myanmar who never looks up, with the girl who shares a room with five cousins and still shows up to school every day.

Comfort doesn’t come from everyone being the same. It comes from knowing you won’t be crushed for being different. So how do we build that?

We talk. Not yelling. Not pretending. Just… talking. Like when I finally sat with Mr. Bell—the one with the bottle—and didn’t preach or scold, just said, “You hungry?” Turns out he lost his job after an injury, then his wife, then stopped believing in help. Now sometimes he waters the garden when he’s clear-headed. Small thing. Big deal.

I’ll tell you this—my cousin got hooked on painkillers after his construction accident. He stole from my mom once. Broke her heart. But we didn’t throw him out. We fought for him. Got him treatment. Now he’s back on the job. So when I see someone else struggling? I don’t see “trash.” I see family that maybe nobody’s fighting for yet.

Tolerance? Yeah, we need more. But not the kind that just says, “Fine, do your thing.” The kind that says, “I may not understand, but I see you. And you matter here.”

Because if we only welcome people who look like us, pray like us, live like us—we ain’t building community. We’re building a wall. And walls don’t keep pain out. They just trap it inside.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character43_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*leans forward, voice lower now, more urgent*

Fairness? When jobs are thin and folks are scared—that’s when it gets real. I won’t pretend it’s simple.

I work at the community center part-time—data entry, mostly. Took me two years to get that after the hospital laid me off. I know what it feels like to check your email every hour, hoping for something. So when I see people coming in—newcomers, yes, but also folks from other states, even Americans moving here for cheaper rent—I get it. People feel squeezed. Like there’s not enough air to breathe.

But here’s what I believe: fairness isn’t about keeping people *out*. It’s about making sure the game ain’t rigged.

Because let’s be honest—the reason jobs feel scarce ain’t always because of migrants. It’s because wages haven’t moved since 2015. Because one rich landlord owns six blocks and doesn’t fix a damn thing. Because the factory closed and they built a warehouse where you work 12 hours for temp pay and no benefits. That’s who’s really stealing opportunity—from *everyone*.

Now, do some newcomers take cash jobs under the table, no taxes, no protections? Yes. And that hurts. Because then the guy down the street says, “Why should I pay minimum wage when Ramón will do it for less?” That’s not fair—to him, to us, to Ramón. Nobody wins.

So if I had a say? I’d say: Let people come, but make the rules clear. Everyone pays in. Everyone follows labor laws. No cheating the system. And while we’re at it—enforce those rules on the *bosses*, not just the workers. Fine the contractors who exploit both locals and migrants. That’s fairness.

And protect the bottom. If we only have 10 janitor jobs and 50 people want them, don’t let wages drop to $6 an hour just because someone’s desperate. That drags us all down. Raise the floor so nobody’s begging.

Also—train people. I did that HVAC course at the technical college—ISCED Level 4, yeah, not fancy, but it got me work for years. Why aren’t we offering that to more folks? Locals *and* newcomers? Teach English, teach skills, help people move up. Then it’s not a race to the bottom—it’s a ladder.

And one more thing: don’t play us against each other. That’s what the powerful want—poor people fighting over crumbs while they eat steak. My neighbor says, “They’re taking our jobs,” but “they” is usually another poor person just trying to survive. The real “they”? The ones with the money, the ones who never worry about losing anything.

So balance? It’s not about numbers. It’s about dignity. Let people work—but make sure the work respects us all. Keep doors open, but guard the value of labor like it’s sacred. Because it is.

We’ve all got families to feed. Mine’s been here three generations. His might’ve arrived last month. But when the lights go out and the stomach growls? Hunger don’t care about papers.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character43_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*sits back, folds her arms loosely, voice steady but with a quiet intensity*

When I hear all these voices on the radio, the politicians shouting, the neighbors arguing—it feels like everyone’s talking *past* each other. Like we’ve forgotten how to listen while still holding our ground.

Let me start with what I *know*—not from TV, but from life.

Yes, immigrants fill jobs people don’t want. I see it every day. The nursing home down the street? Half the aides are from Honduras or the Philippines. Who else is gonna sit up all night with old Mrs. Lopez when she can’t sleep, changing her pad, singing her lullabies in Spanish? Not many locals applying for that job at $13 an hour, no benefits. Same with farms, with meatpacking, with dishwashers in diners open till 2 a.m. These aren’t lazy jobs—they’re hard. And if you kicked every immigrant out tomorrow, those positions wouldn’t magically go to “real Americans.” They’d just stay empty—or get filled by machines, and then nobody has work.

So that part? True. Vital. Fact.

Now, culture. My mom used to say, “La comida abre el corazón.” Food opens the heart. You know what saved this neighborhood? When that Guatemalan woman opened her little pupuseria in the old laundromat. Now kids from every block run there after school. You hear Kreyòl, Arabic, English, Spanglish—all laughing over fried plantains. That’s not a threat. That’s life getting richer. We ain’t losing our identity—we’re adding to it. Like layers in a stew. You don’t throw out the beans because you added cilantro.

But then—security. That one… sits heavy.

I won’t pretend I don’t worry. When my niece walks home late, yeah, I check my phone. When the news says someone got jumped near the bus stop, and they mention he came from somewhere overseas—I feel that knot in my chest. But then I ask: Is he here legally? Did he come as a refugee? What happened to him before he got here? And more importantly—what about the *citizen* who robbed the corner store last week? Or the cop who beat that kid last year?

Crime? It exists. But pinning it on immigrants—that’s too easy. I’ve seen studies now—real ones, from the university extension office—showing immigrants commit crimes at *lower* rates than native-born. Hard to believe? Maybe. But I looked at the data myself. So maybe what we fear isn’t the stranger—but the unknown. And fear grows when leaders stoke it instead of teaching us how to be safe *together*.

Terrorism? That word gets thrown around like trash. One Yemeni family moved in last winter—quiet, religious, running a taxi service. Then some graffiti appeared: “Go back.” Their daughter stopped coming to the garden. Why? Because of something that happened 2,000 miles away ten years ago? That ain’t justice. That’s punishment without trial.

Humanitarian side—this one speaks to my soul. Because I remember my tío, how he fled the gangs in San Salvador with nothing but his shoes. He wasn’t rich. Wasn’t political. Just wanted to live. If someone had slammed the door in his face, I wouldn’t be here. My kids wouldn’t exist. So when I see families sleeping in tents at the border, kids wrapped in foil blankets—I don’t see “invaders.” I see *us*. Our past. Our luck reversed.

And yes—some people worry wages drop. That’s real pain. But again, let’s name the real enemy: greedy bosses. Not the guy picking tomatoes next to you. The man who owns the field paying both of you poverty wages so he can drive a Mercedes. He doesn’t care if you were born here or crossed the river—he just wants cheap hands.

So which views are reasonable?

All of them have a seed of truth—except the ones built on hate.

We need labor? Yes.  
We gain from diversity? Yes.  
We should be safe? Absolutely.  
We must help the desperate? God, yes.

But the fear that says “close the door completely”? That needs more facts. More dialogue. More sitting across from someone different and asking, “What’s your story?” Instead of assuming.

I think if we spent half as much time building bridges as we do building fences, we’d all sleep better.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character43_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*leans in, voice low but clear, like she’s sharing something hard-won*

I don’t believe in open borders. Not because I don’t care—but because I *do*. Because I know what chaos looks like. I’ve seen it—when people come with nothing, no plan, and end up sleeping in basements, getting exploited, kids missing school, families torn apart by fear. That ain’t dignity. That ain’t fairness.

And I sure as hell don’t believe in shutting the door completely. Refusing all workers? That’s cruelty dressed up as protection. It hurts us all—economically, morally. My own family didn’t come on a visa with a ribbon. We came because we had to. So no, I won’t say “not here” to someone just trying to survive.

If I had a say? I’d go with a mix: **admit people based on job demand**, yes—but not just any job. Real jobs. With real wages. With labor protections. No more of this “Oh, we need farmhands,” then paying them under the table so locals can’t compete and immigrants have no rights. That system? It’s rigged. Fix it first.

Set **fair numerical limits**—not arbitrary numbers pulled from politics, but based on what our communities can actually absorb. Not just housing, not just schools, but *belonging*. Can we help these people integrate? Do we have ESL classes? Job training? Mental health support for those who’ve fled war or trauma?

Too many come, and we just… dump them. Then when things get hard, we blame *them* for not fitting in. That’s not their failure. That’s ours.

So yeah—limits. But humane ones. And space within those limits for refugees. Always. Not quotas that treat human suffering like math. When there’s a crisis—a coup, a hurricane, gang takeover—we make room. Like El Salvador did for Nicaraguans during Ortega’s crackdown. We remember we’re not immune.

And here’s what nobody talks about enough: **pathways**. A migrant worker should be able to stay, earn, learn English, pay taxes—and after ten years of clean record, fair wage, community involvement? They apply for permanent status. No back of the line forever. If you’ve built your life here, raised kids here, paid into the system—then you’re not “foreign.” You’re family.

That’s how integration happens. Not by force. By time. By dignity.

And protect local workers too. Make sure no employer hires migrants *because* they’ll accept less. Enforce wage laws. Invest in trade schools—like the one I went to—so if someone loses a job, they can retrain. Don’t leave people behind while blaming immigrants for the fall.

Fairness? It means rules that apply to *everyone*—bosses, locals, newcomers. No cheating. No scapegoating.

A balanced policy, to me, looks like a strong gate with an open hand. Screen people in safely. Help them stand on their own feet. Let contribution lead to belonging.

Because this country? It was never meant to be static. It’s supposed to grow. Just not at the cost of crushing the most vulnerable—or forgetting who we used to be.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character43_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character43_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*pauses for a long moment, eyes glistening, voice softer now—less performance, more revelation*

Honestly… I thought I knew her well. We talked for years—over coffee, at rallies, sitting on that same garden bench where we used to split an empanada. But doing this today—speaking *as* her, not just *about* her—I felt something shift.

I realized… she didn’t just *have* opinions. She carried them like scars and stitches. Every word was tied to a face, a name, a memory. It wasn’t abstract. It was personal. Like when she talked about refugees—she wasn’t thinking of “policy.” She was seeing her cousin’s boy, the one who disappeared for six months during the gang sweeps in Soyapango. That changed how I hear the word “border” now. It’s not a line on a map. It’s someone’s child walking it barefoot.

And I’ll admit—I’ve been more afraid than I let on. Afraid that if we keep letting people in, there won’t be enough. For my son. For his future. But stepping into her shoes today… I saw how small that fear looks next to her hope. Her stubborn belief that community isn’t something you’re born into—it’s something you build, brick by brick, with people you didn’t choose.

She never dismissed the struggles of locals. Never said, “Just deal with it.” But she also refused to see newcomers as threats. To her, both were caught in the same broken system. And instead of choosing sides, she wanted to fix the game.

That’s what moved me most—her refusal to hate. Even when she was tired. Even when she was scared.

Doing this… it didn’t change my mind so much as deepen it. Like roots going further down. I still worry about jobs, about strain on schools, about safety. But now I carry her question with me: *“Are we solving the real problem—or just punishing the wrong people?”*

And I realize—honoring her isn’t just remembering her laugh or how she always brought extra tortillas. It’s living like she did. With open eyes. A guarded heart, maybe—but one willing to stretch.

So thank you. Not just for inviting me to speak as her. For giving me a chance to *listen* to her again. Because today, I didn’t just play a role.  
I remembered a friend.  
And I found my way back to hope.
